newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia capex seen on track despite Q4 fall.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia capex seen on track despite Q4 fall.

text.p: Australia's investment outlook, a key pillar of the stronger growth expectations for 1997, looks quite secure despite a weaker than expected performance in the December quarter, economists said.

Official data showed on Thursday that private new capital expenditure (capex) fell 2.4 percent in the December quarter, with building and structures down 7.7 percent and equipment, plant and machinery up 0.1 percent in the quarter.
Forecasts had centred on a 2.1 percent rise, and only ranged as low as a 2.0 percent fall.

The Bureau of Statistics said December quarter capex was affected by the delaying of some significiant projects, particularly construction projects in the mining, transport and storage industries, and some other projects running behind schedule.
Despite the quarterly fall, total capex levels were still 19.6 percent up on their December 1995 levels.
Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said the news of the quarterly fall may have initially made some people nervous about the likelihood of achieving the government's forecasts.

Last month the government upgraded the forecast for investment in 1996/97 (July/June) to 17 percent from an already robust 14 percent, and it is seen as the key to achieving the forecast 3.5 percent growth rate.
In fact, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) last year labelled investment "the linchpin of forecast growth."
"But you look at the expectations numbers, and actually expectations are up," Henderson said. "So that more than supports the government's 17 percent forecast.
The survey contained two projections of expected expenditure which showed firms remained optimistic on investment.

"There is a very strong momentum in capital expenditure expectations, which is very important going forward, and it validates the sort of view the Reserve Bank was expressing that there is still quite a strong recovery underway," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell senior economist Bruce Hockman said.
The December quarter survey forecast for investment in the 1996/97 year was 1.5 percent above the September estimate for 1996/97, and 11.8 percent over the corresponding estimate for 1995/96.
The survey also contained the first estimate for 1997/98, and it was 10.1 percent above the same estimate for 1996/97.

Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said the capex data and the outlook for 1996/97 were a bit weaker than he had expected, although he still saw strong growth in the year. The strength of expectations for 97/98 was surprising, however.
"That was a bit stronger than I was expecting and I think sets the scene for a continuing pretty good growth picture over next year as well," he said.

The figures validated the RBA's view that growth would be driven by investment, aided by a positive assessment by business on the economy's prosects and "being supported by relatively favourable financial conditions."
"The cuts in interest rates in the second half of 1996 are cleary working," Macquarie Bank senior economist John Kyriakopoulos said.

The combination of investment looking strong into 1998, and other indicators of economic activity showing signs of strength while inflation and price pressures were remaining moderate, supported the market view the official interest rates were on hold for the time being at 6.00 percent, economists said.
